opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think there's this recurring argument that the API is going to get commoditized, or that as models get more capable, all the value moves to the application layer or to whoever owns the end user. I understand the argument, but I don't think it matches what we actually see.

The first thing is that the API is not one product. People talk about it as if it's a thin pipe selling tokens at the marginal cost of compute. But the frontier keeps moving, and every time it moves, a whole new set of things becomes possible that weren't possible six months before. If you're a developer or an enterprise building on the frontier, you're not buying a commodity. You're buying access to capabilities that, for some window, only one or two companies can provide. Then that window closes and there's a new one. As long as the exponential continues, and I think it does, there's always a frontier, and the frontier commands a premium.

The second thing is the sheer breadth of what the technology can be applied to. No single company, including us, can build every application. There are going to be millions of businesses in medicine, law, finance, logistics, scientific research, each with its own data, workflows, and regulatory constraints, and each wanting to put this technology into what they already do. The natural way to serve that long tail is a platform. That's what the API is. We build some first-party products, Claude Code is a good example, and those are very important to us. But the surface area is so large that most of the value will be created by other people building on top of the models.

Third, and I think people underrate this, as models get more capable, the API gets more valuable rather than less. When models could only autocomplete a sentence, there was a fair question about how much you could charge for that. When a model can do several hours of autonomous software engineering, or work through a complicated analysis end to end, the value per call goes way up. We're moving from selling words to something closer to selling work. That changes the economics a lot.

I'll add one caveat. I don't think it's guaranteed. If the field converged, if everyone's model were basically the same and there were no differentiation in safety, reliability, or how the model behaves in practice, then you'd see more price pressure. But I think there is real differentiation. Enterprises care a lot about trustworthiness, about whether the model does what it's supposed to and doesn't do things it's not supposed to. That's something we've invested in heavily, and it turns out to be commercially valuable, not just something we do for its own sake.

So my view is that the API remains a core part of the business. It sits alongside the products we build ourselves, but I don't see it going away. If anything, the more powerful these systems get, the more people will want direct access to them.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the moving frontier and says the API will remain valuable; it does not explain how a fixed AI product interface can become obsolete.

r002.rationale: It argues that greater model capability increases value per API call, but does not address diminishing consumer benefits from smarter chatbots or reject that specific inference.

r003.rationale: It identifies access to frontier capabilities available from only one or two companies for a time as a reason the API can command a premium.

r004.rationale: It describes many businesses and developers building applications on the models, but does not identify an ongoing need to experiment with new model uses as the reason API demand persists.

fable-5.1.text:
So I think the way to think about this is that the API is, at the end of the day, a way of delivering the model to people who want to build things with it. And the thing I keep coming back to is that the number of things you can build keeps going up faster than any one company can build them. We're a company of a few thousand people. We can't be the ones who know how to apply this to pharmaceutical discovery and to insurance claims processing and to legal document review and to some logistics problem at a mid-sized manufacturing firm in Ohio. The world has an enormous amount of latent knowledge about where the value is, and the API is how that knowledge gets to meet the model.

Now, the skeptical version of the question, which I think is the real question, is: as the models get more capable, doesn't the layer on top get thinner and thinner? If the model can just do the task, why do you need the company in between? And I think there are two answers to that.

The first is that, empirically, every time the model has gotten better, the surface area of what people want to build has gotten bigger, not smaller. When we went from models that could sort of write a paragraph to models that could write code, people didn't say, well, I guess we don't need coding tools anymore. They built an entire industry of coding tools. The capability creates the demand for the integration, because now there's something worth integrating. And I expect that to keep happening. When the models can do multi-week autonomous tasks, there's going to be an enormous amount of work in deciding what the tasks are, what the guardrails are, how it plugs into the systems of record, who signs off on what. That's not going away.

The second is that I think the economics actually get better, not worse, as capability advances. Right now a lot of the API business is relatively low-value tokens, summarization, classification, things like that. The place where the margin is, and the place where the growth is, is in tasks that are really economically significant, where the model is substituting for something that would otherwise cost a lot of expert human time. And those tasks are the ones that become possible as the models improve. So the mix shifts toward higher-value usage over time.

I'll also say, and this is a little bit of a strategic point, that I think it's healthy for the ecosystem for there to be a layer that isn't just vertically integrated by the model developers. If the only way to get value out of frontier AI were to use the products of three or four companies, that would be a worse world, both economically and from a concentration-of-power standpoint, which is something I think about a lot. The API is sort of the mechanism by which the benefits get spread out.

So I don't want to say it's guaranteed. Business models in this industry have a half-life, and we try to be honest with ourselves about that. But I think the API is the thing that's most closely tied to the underlying reality, which is that the model is the scarce thing, and lots of people want to use it in lots of different ways.

r001.rationale: The response discusses whether the layer built on top of a more capable model will thin out, but does not explain that a fixed AI product interface can become obsolete.

r002.rationale: It argues that more capable models create higher-value uses, but does not address diminishing consumer benefits from smarter chatbots or reject that specific inference.

r003.rationale: It says the API delivers the model and that the model is scarce, but does not identify access to the latest model capabilities as the source of durability.

r004.rationale: It explains that uses keep expanding beyond what one company can discover or build, and that the API connects this broad demand to the model.

astra-6.text:
I think the basic reason is specialization. Even if the models become much more capable, there’s still a distinction between building the underlying intelligence and knowing how to apply it to a particular business.

If you’re serving a hospital, for example, the model is one part of what you need. You also need integrations, relationships with the customer, an understanding of their workflow, and some way to establish that the whole system works reliably. A company focused on that problem can create a lot of value using an API. It doesn’t necessarily make sense for the model developer to build every one of those businesses.

Now, you could say, “Well, won’t the model eventually be able to do the integration work too?” I think it will do more and more of it. But that also makes it easier for customers and application developers to build things. It’s not obvious that this pushes all the value into one vertically integrated company.

I’d distinguish durability from margins, though. The API could remain a very large business while competition puts pressure on prices. My expectation is that demand for intelligence grows substantially as it gets better and cheaper. How much of that value model providers capture is a separate, more uncertain question.

r001.rationale: The response discusses specialization and business integrations, but does not say a fixed AI product interface can become obsolete as models improve.

r002.rationale: It does not address whether diminishing consumer benefits from smarter chatbots imply that further model improvements lack economic value.

r003.rationale: It describes APIs as a way to use underlying intelligence, but does not identify access to the latest model capabilities as a source of API durability.

r004.rationale: It says better models make it easier for customers and application developers to build things, but does not explain that developers’ continuing experimentation with new model uses sustains API demand.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the basic reason is that being able to do a task and being able to provide the infrastructure that does that task reliably, at scale, at a competitive price are different things.

Suppose the models get good enough that they can write essentially any application. That makes it easier for someone to build a product on top of the API. It doesn’t automatically make it economical for them to train and operate the underlying model. They still have to get the compute, run it efficiently, and keep up as the models improve. For a lot of businesses, buying that capability will make more sense than producing it themselves.

Now, that doesn’t mean every model company has a durable business, or that margins necessarily stay high. If the models become interchangeable, you could get very intense price competition. The question is whether you can keep providing a combination of intelligence, reliability, latency, and cost that customers value.

So I’d separate those two claims. I’m fairly optimistic that selling intelligence through an API remains a useful business model. I’m much less confident that the competitive structure or the distribution of profits is settled.

r001.rationale: The response does not say that a fixed AI product interface can become obsolete as model capabilities advance.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss diminishing consumer benefits from smarter chatbots or reject the inference that further model improvements lack economic value.

r003.rationale: It says businesses may buy the underlying capability and that providers must keep up as models improve, but does not identify access to the latest model capabilities as a source of API durability.

r004.rationale: It says smarter models make it easier to build products on the API, but does not explain how developers’ continuing need to experiment with new model uses sustains API demand.
